newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia moves to end row over Surgut share issue.
newsitem.headline: Russia moves to end row over Surgut share issue.

text.p: Russia moved on Tuesday to bolster shareholder rights infringed in a controversial share issue by oil company AO Surgutneftegaz and to end uncertainty about the ownership of another large oil company, Sidanko.
The Federal Commission for the Securities Market said Surgut management had agreed to take steps to put right violations of securities law which arose as a result of last October's issue.

"In addition to addressing technical questions of getting value for the shares that were sold, it appears to answer a broader question of whether shareholders have rights in Russia," said Renaissance Capital energy analyst James Bunch.

Surgut Holding acquired the issue of 500 million ordinary shares and 34.02 million preferred shares in its AO Surgutneftegaz SNGS.RTS 0#SNGS.RUO production unit, raising its stake to 43.5 percent from 38 percent.

The commission said Surgut would convene an extraordinary shareholders' meeting of AO Surgutneftegaz which would give holders of voting stock preferential rights to acquire ordinary shares in proportion to their holdings.
Surgut Holding and its investment vehicle, Surgut Investments, would pay an additional 200 billion roubles ($36 million) for the shares.
Surgut Investments would pay an additional 168 billion roubles for 420 million shares and the commission spokesman said this would raise the share price to the market level.
Surgutneftegaz share prices rose on the announcement. Its ordinary shares were at $0.413 at 1400 GMT after $0.405 and the preferred shares rose to $0.290 from $0.276.
The disputed issue effectively diluted existing holdings in Surgutneftegaz and helped depress the entire market.
"By and large this is a good thing and Surgutneftegaz's underlying performance is such that people will want exposure to it," said analyst Jim Nail of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The Federal Property Fund said a 51 percent stake in Sidanko would be sold by January 9 at a starting price of $129 million.
MFK bank, which is associated with the powerful Uneximbank banking group, won the right last year to manage a 51 percent stake in Sidanko under a government shares-for-loans scheme.
MFK won the original auction with a $130 million bid.

The winner must also invest $161 million in Sidanko and hand over 73.70 million shares in a Siberian refinery in which Sidanko already has a 38 percent stake. Sidanko owns large stakes in three big oil producers -- Chernogorneft, Kondpetroleum and Varyoganneftegaz.
Analysts said the Uneximbank group was likely to bid.
"I couldn't see how it could not be someone sponsored by Uneximbank," said CentreInvest Securities research head James Fenkner. "I couldn't see why Uneximbank would give something like that up."
Interros Oil, affiliated with the Interros financial- industrial group built around Uneximbank, in September won a 34 percent stake in Sidanko at an investment tender.
The Sidanko stake is the second in the shares-for-loans scheme to be offered for sale. A 33.3 percent stake in oil group Yukos is to be auctioned at a starting price of $160 million.
The shares-for-loans scheme proved controversial with auction winners often close to the organisers and winning bids close to the starting prices.
"The goal of the loans for shares was to acquire the trusteeship and then eventually the ownership. That is why the fight was so tough last year," said Fenkner.
Fenkner said that settling the ownership issues could have a positive impact on the stock involved.
"Getting rid of this uncertainty will move the company more on to a traditional valuation basis," he said. ($1=5526 Rouble)
